title: Mount Makiling
subtitle: Sinag ng Lupa: the Ray of Earth
intro: Mount Makiling looks asleep from Los Baños, but today it is holding its breath.
Maria Makiling has watched over this mountain since before there were roads. Her rules are simple: take only what you need, and take your trash home.
The anino, the shadows, did not read the rules. A kapre in the old balete tree has gone wild and is throwing rocks at everybody.
Make a fist. The ground will listen.
outro: Maria Makiling nods once, which from her is a hug.
'The next ray is downriver, in the gorge. Mang Amado is waiting. He will overcharge you.'

boss_lines.intro: The balete shakes. A kapre climbs down, still smoking his enormous cigar. He does not look friendly.
boss_lines.phase2: He swings a whole branch like a bat. The ground starts to give way.
boss_lines.phase3: The cigar glows red. He is done warning you.
boss_lines.defeat: The kapre sits down hard and coughs, and the shadow slides off him. 'Sorry,' he mutters. 'Bad few days.'

lore: Mount Makiling, in Laguna, is said to be watched over by Maria Makiling, a diwata who rewards the kind and hides from the greedy.
A kapre is a giant who lives in big trees, usually seen smoking an enormous cigar. Most of them are harmless. This one is not himself.

title: Pagsanjan Gorge
subtitle: Sinag ng Tubig: the Ray of Water
intro: The Pagsanjan gorge is where boatmen pole tourists up the rapids for a living. Lately the rapids have started pushing back.
Mang Amado has paddled this river for forty years. He has opinions about the water, and about your life jacket.
He is holding the second ray in a biscuit tin, and the shadows want the tin.
Open your hand flat. Water does not fight the rock; it goes around it.
outro: Mang Amado hands over the tin. 'No charge,' he says, then adds a boarding fee.
'The next one is far north, on a windy island with a lighthouse. Bring a jacket.'

boss_lines.intro: Something scaly rises from the pool below the falls. The siyokoy are river folk, and this one has had enough of visitors.
boss_lines.phase2: He slams the water, and the whole gorge answers.
boss_lines.phase3: He dives. Watch where the water moves.
boss_lines.defeat: The Siyokoy King slides back under, embarrassed. The river runs clear again.

lore: Pagsanjan Falls, in Laguna, is reached by narrow boats poled upstream by boatmen who know every rock in the gorge.
A siyokoy is a scaly water creature of Philippine folklore, usually described as a merman with a bad temper.

title: Basco Lighthouse
subtitle: Sinag ng Hangin: the Ray of Wind
intro: Batanes is the northernmost province: green rolling hills, stone houses, and a wind that never takes a day off.
Ate Luz has kept the Basco lighthouse for most of her life. Luz means light. She says it is a coincidence.
A typhoon has been parked over the island since the dark began, and the ray is at the top of the tower.
Close your palm tight. Wind gets through anything that is not braced for it.
outro: The lamp turns, and its beam finally reaches the sea.
Ate Luz points south. 'Taal. Take a hat. No, not for the sun. There is no sun.'

boss_lines.intro: The clouds close into a ring. The eye of the storm is looking straight at you.
boss_lines.phase2: The wind picks up every loose thing on the island and throws it your way.
boss_lines.phase3: The eye closes. This is the part where it gets worse.
boss_lines.defeat: The storm unwinds into an ordinary, clear sky. Ate Luz switches the lamp on and says, 'Finally.'

lore: The Basco Lighthouse, on Naidi Hills, looks out over Batan Island in Batanes, one of the windiest places in the country.
About twenty typhoons enter the Philippine area each year. Filipinos call them bagyo, and tie the roof down.

title: Taal Island
subtitle: Sinag ng Apoy: the Ray of Fire
intro: Taal is a volcano on an island in a lake inside an older volcano's crater. You could not make that geography up.
Tatay Berting farms fish beside it. He has evacuated three times and come back a fourth, because the fish do not feed themselves.
The fourth ray is at the crater, and the ground there is already warm.
Two fingers up. Fire answers people who are not afraid of it, or who are afraid and go anyway.
outro: The ray flares gold. Four are home.
The fifth is not a place. It is wherever the dragon went.

boss_lines.intro: The crater lake boils. The blaze climbs out of it in a shape that looks, rudely, a lot like a face.
boss_lines.phase2: Ash begins to fall. It is hot enough to count as rain.
boss_lines.phase3: It is burning its own ray to keep you out. Water hurts it most.
boss_lines.defeat: The blaze sinks back into the crater and the lake goes quiet. Somewhere a rooster, finally, crows.

lore: Taal Volcano is a small volcano on an island in Taal Lake, in Batangas, and one of the most active in the Philippines.
Its last major eruption was in January 2020. The families who live around the lake have been rebuilding ever since.

title: Mouth of the Bakunawa
subtitle: Ang Huling Sinag: the Last Ray
intro: There is no place called the Bakunawa's mouth. There is only the dark, and the sound of something very large breathing.
Four rays hang around you like lanterns. The sun and the moon are in there somewhere, behind the teeth.
Your hands know the fifth sign, the one Lola Auring never explained: lightning. It is what Bathala sends to things that will not listen.
And you know what the elders do when the moon is eaten. Press your palms together. Make noise.
outro: Dawn. The first one anyone has seen in three days.
It looks a little crooked, like it has been through something. So have you.

boss_lines.intro: The Bakunawa uncoils out of the dark with the sun and the moon glowing in its throat.
boss_lines.phase2: It roars, and for a second every light in the world flickers.
boss_lines.phase3: It is gulping again. Press your palms together. Kalampag!
boss_lines.defeat: The Bakunawa chokes. The moon comes out first, then the sun, then a great deal of seawater. Far away someone is banging a pot, and then a hundred someones are.

lore: In the old stories the Bakunawa is a sea dragon that swallows the moon, and the elders drive it off by banging pots and pans until it spits the moon back out.
Some tellings say there were once seven moons. The Bakunawa ate six.
